title: What were the black codes?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Black Codes, the series of laws passed by Southern states in 1865-1866 after the Civil War to restrict newly freed Black Americans and recreate the plantation labor system. They cover the end of the Civil War and Lincoln's assassination, President Andrew Johnson's Presidential Reconstruction and the Freedmen's Bureau, the "forty acres and a mule" rumors and Sherman's Field Order No. 15, labor contracts and debt peonage, vagrancy and apprenticeship laws, Mississippi's pig laws, the Thirteenth Amendment's convict-labor loophole, congressional Radical Reconstruction, the rise of Black officeholders, the abandonment of Reconstruction, and links to Jim Crow and later prison labor. The episode ends with a listener letter from Ian Clarkson.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode pick
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode, a listener pick on the Black Codes, and mentions sources including the Constitutional Rights Foundation and the Mississippi Encyclopedia.

segments.title: What the Black Codes were and the end of the Civil War
segments.summary: The Black Codes are defined as laws Southern white leaders passed to re-enslave or restrict freed people and keep the plantation labor system. The hosts discuss slave codes, the end of the Civil War, and Lincoln's assassination five days later.

segments.title: Andrew Johnson and the Freedmen's Bureau
segments.summary: After Lincoln's death, Andrew Johnson took over and favored a lenient reentry plan. The Freedmen's Bureau was set up to help freed people with wages, jobs and courts, which white Southerners resented. Johnson's plan let white men form new state governments.

segments.title: Southern state conventions and segregated schools
segments.summary: Southern states held elections in 1865 and wrote new constitutions and Black Codes. Former Confederate leaders regained power, and the new legislatures created free public schools for white children only.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts take a short break.

segments.title: Forty acres and a mule
segments.summary: Rumors spread in Black and white communities around Christmas 1865 about land redistribution. The hosts trace the forty acres idea to Sherman's Field Order No. 15, which was never fulfilled, and to land Johnson's plan returned to former owners.

segments.title: Labor contracts, debt peonage and vagrancy laws
segments.summary: Black Codes such as South Carolina's labor contracts forced freed people into servant contracts with long hours and limited movement. Store credit led to debt peonage, whipping was allowed for servants, and vagrancy arrests fed workers into a cycle of debt tied to plantation owners.

segments.title: Apprenticeship laws, unequal courts and penalties
segments.summary: Apprenticeship laws let officials bind Black children to work without pay. The hosts describe unequal courts, harsher penalties for Black defendants, and the convict-leasing case of Green Cottenham in Alabama.

segments.title: Mississippi pig laws and the Thirteenth Amendment loophole
segments.summary: Mississippi's pig laws made stealing farm animals grand larceny, and the hosts explain how the Thirteenth Amendment exception for punishment for crime let states arrest Black people en masse. They note that prison labor continued, citing a 2005 figure.

segments.title: Radical Reconstruction, Johnson's veto and the fall of Reconstruction
segments.summary: Congress rejected the Southern states' new laws. Radical Republicans pushed Reconstruction, and Johnson vetoed the Civil Rights Act of 1866. The hosts describe Black voting and officeholding, the constitutional amendments, the KKK's terror campaign, and how Northern support faded, opening the door to Jim Crow.

segments.title: Legacy and further viewing and reading
segments.summary: The hosts connect the Black Codes to modern attitudes and recommend the HBO documentary Exterminate All the Brutes and the Jacobin article Killing Reconstruction by Heather Cox Richardson.

segments.title: Listener mail from Ian Clarkson
segments.summary: Josh reads a letter of thanks from long-time listener Ian Clarkson of Dallas, who says the show helped during COVID and compares the hosts to Click and Clack.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and give the email address for listener contact.
